tldr: By considering not only GPU parallelism but also memory hierarchies, the authors developed "CUDA MPC," which fuses the entire iterative optimization loop into a single CUDA kernel. It achieves up to a 965x speedup compared to tensor implementations like PyTorch, successfully solving complex, long-horizon nonlinear robotics problems—such as centralized control of a 10-agent swarm—in real time, where conventional CPU solvers fail to keep up.
hero_caption: Architecture comparison between existing GPU optimization using tensor frameworks like PyTorch (left) and the proposed CUDA MPC (right). Instead of round-tripping between host and device at every iteration, CUDA MPC launches the entire optimization loop as a single fused kernel, retaining variables in on-chip shared memory to complete computations entirely on-chip.
overview:
Model Predictive Control (MPC) is a powerful method that strictly handles constraints. However, when dealing with fast robots, multi-agent systems, or long prediction horizons, the computational burden of online optimization becomes a severe bottleneck. While GPU acceleration has been explored in recent years, relying on frameworks like PyTorch launches countless small CUDA kernels per iteration and causes frequent reads and writes to slow global memory (VRAM), preventing the GPU from achieving its full potential.

To address this, the authors propose "CUDA MPC," a GPU-native MPC solver that co-designs the optimization algorithm (parallel-in-horizon ADMM) with CUDA hardware characteristics (shared memory and block structures). Drawing inspiration from FlashAttention to drastically eliminate memory I/O bottlenecks, it packs the iterative optimization across the entire horizon into a single fused kernel, keeping variables resident in fast on-chip shared memory. Furthermore, by using lightweight atomic flags to locally synchronize only temporally adjacent blocks, it achieves high-efficiency synchronization that does not depend on the number of blocks.

In benchmarks, CUDA MPC achieved up to a 965x speedup over a PyTorch implementation of the same algorithm. Across six nonlinear benchmarks—including car parking and 10-drone swarm control—it solved problems with prediction horizons 1 to 2 orders of magnitude longer than CPU solvers like acados and CasADi within sampling intervals. It successfully solved complex tasks without collisions, whereas existing methods either could not run in real time or were trapped in local minima.
contributions: Built "CUDA MPC," a GPU-native MPC architecture that fuses the entire iterative solve of parallel-in-horizon ADMM into a single CUDA kernel and completes computation on on-chip shared memory
Devised a localized atomic-flag synchronization protocol that eliminates heavy grid-wide barriers and coordinates only adjacent temporal blocks with low overhead
Demonstrated up to a 965x speedup over tensor-framework implementations and a drastic reduction in VRAM access traffic from gigabytes down to megabytes
Demonstrated long-horizon real-time computation and superior closed-loop control performance outperforming existing CPU/GPU solvers across six nonlinear robotics problems

sections.heading: Why didn't MPC get faster just by using a GPU?
sections.summary: MPC is an excellent control method, but compute time explodes as prediction horizons and state dimensions grow. Simply moving to GPUs via PyTorch stalls due to kernel launch overhead and VRAM latency, making dedicated hardware-optimized design essential.
sections.details:
Model Predictive Control (MPC) is a highly reliable control method that solves finite-horizon optimization problems while explicitly considering state and input constraints. Its use has expanded to autonomous vehicles and fast drones, but it faces strict timing constraints requiring optimization problems (QPs or NLPs) to be solved within a sampling interval.

Prominent CPU solvers such as acados and CasADi skillfully exploit sparse problem structures. However, as the horizon length or system dimension grows, computational costs surge, forcing compromises with shorter prediction horizons.

One might think that using GPUs with thousands of cores would solve this, but it is not that simple. Implementing iterative algorithms like ADMM in tensor frameworks such as PyTorch or JAX triggers thousands of fine-grained kernel launches per iteration, each reading and writing intermediate data to slow global memory (VRAM). This overhead completely wipes out the benefits of parallelization.

To tackle this challenge, this paper proposes CUDA MPC, which unifies the algorithm, execution model, and memory structure. Just as FlashAttention dramatically accelerated large language models by minimizing memory I/O, CUDA MPC unleashes true GPU parallelism by fusing the entire optimization loop into a single CUDA kernel and keeping variables resident in low-latency shared memory.

sections.heading: How it differs from previous CPU and GPU MPC approaches
sections.summary: CPU solvers are bottlenecked by sequential dependencies, while existing GPU methods suffer from tensor framework overhead or the communication cost of global scans. CUDA MPC fundamentally breaks these constraints via ADMM temporal splitting and block-local synchronization.
sections.details:
Prior work broadly splits into CPU-based solvers and GPU-accelerated solvers.

### II-A CPU-Based MPC Solvers
Mainstream real-time nonlinear MPC relies on CasADi (coupled with Ipopt, etc.) and acados (using SQP-RTI or HPIPM). These thoroughly exploit problem structure using block-sparse matrix factorizations or Riccati recursions. However, sequential dependencies along the time horizon remain, leading to computational costs that scale serially with horizon length. First-order methods like TinyMPC and OSQP are effective on CPUs, but they are not designed to solve large-scale nonlinear MPC in a time-parallel fashion.

### II-B GPU-Accelerated MPC
A common GPU approach in robotics is sampling-based MPPI (Model Predictive Path Integral). However, MPPI is gradient-free, causing the required number of samples to explode as input dimensions grow, and it cannot strictly guarantee satisfaction of inequality constraints.

Gradient-based GPU approaches include methods that kernelize only linear solver routines (e.g., MPCGPU) and methods that run ADMM on top of PyTorch (such as ReLU-QP or πMPC). However, the former cannot exploit temporal parallelism, while the latter suffers from framework-induced kernel launch overhead and VRAM traffic. Other attempts use associative scans to parallelize across the time horizon, but back-and-forth scans and synchronizations across the entire horizon remain a heavy burden.

CUDA MPC keeps each stage's computation independent via temporal ADMM splitting while restricting consensus exchanges solely to adjacent blocks. This eliminates global scans and achieves ultra-fast optimization self-contained within a single kernel.

sections.heading: Mathematical formulation for solving nonlinear problems in parallel across time
sections.summary: Using sequential convex programming (SCP) to approximate nonlinear dynamics and non-convex constraints as polyhedra, combined with a velocity-form input definition and ADMM consensus splitting, the problem is decomposed into convex subproblems that can be solved completely in parallel along the time horizon.
sections.details:
The background theory enabling CUDA MPC to quickly solve MPC problems with nonlinear dynamics and non-convex constraints is as follows:

### IV-A Sequential Convexification
To solve nonlinear MPC, Sequential Convex Programming (SCP) is adopted. Nonlinear dynamics are linearized around the previous outer-iteration trajectory via first-order Taylor expansion, and nonlinear state and input constraints are convexified into stage-wise polyhedral approximation sets. The outer loop repeats until convergence criteria are met or the maximum iteration count $j_{\max}$ is reached.

### IV-B Incremental-Input Formulation
A velocity-form formulation is used by introducing input increments $\Delta\mathbf{u}_k = \mathbf{u}_k - \mathbf{u}_{k-1}$. By defining an augmented state $\bar{\mathbf{x}}_k$ (dimension $\bar{n}_x = n_x + n_u$) combining state $\mathbf{x}_k$ and previous input $\mathbf{u}_{k-1}$, penalties and constraints on input rates of change are naturally incorporated.

### IV-C Consensus-Split Convex Subproblem
To parallelize across the horizon, consensus splitting via ADMM (the $\pi$MPC framework) is applied. By introducing state copies $\mathbf{z}_{k+1}$ and input copies $\mathbf{v}_k$, QP updates, convex projections, and dynamic consistency updates for each time step are completely decoupled. As a result, projection operations onto the polyhedral convex sets linearized by SCP can be evaluated independently and in parallel across time steps.

sections.heading: Fusing hardware and mathematics: The CUDA MPC architecture
sections.summary: Temporal ADMM is mapped to CUDA thread blocks, completing all optimization iterations within a single fused kernel. Variables remain resident in shared memory, and asynchronous synchronization via atomic flags occurs only between adjacent blocks to achieve ultra-low latency.
sections.details:
CUDA MPC's core architecture tightly couples three tiers: algorithm, execution, and memory.

### V-A Parallel-in-Horizon ADMM
In each outer SCP iteration, the inner ADMM consists of primal updates, constraint projections, and dual updates. Penalty matrices are precomputed upon each linearization. While update equations reference variables from adjacent time steps, they use values from the immediately preceding iteration, enabling completely concurrent evaluation across all time steps $k=0,\ldots,N-1$.

### V-B GPU-Native CUDA Execution and Local Neighbor Synchronization
The prediction horizon $N$ is divided into contiguous subhorizons of length $M$, each assigned to a CUDA thread block (Streaming Multiprocessor, SM). Threads within a block are organized in an $M \times \bar{n}_x$ grid, with each row handling one prediction stage.

The defining feature is kernel fusion: the entire ADMM iteration loop runs within a single custom CUDA kernel. Control is never returned to the host CPU mid-iteration, completely eliminating kernel launch overhead. In addition, CUDA Graphs are applied to outer linearization and trajectory-shifting operations, minimizing CPU dispatch load.

Synchronization is even more critical. Typically, grid-wide GPU synchronization uses `grid.sync()`, which forces all blocks to wait for the slowest block, causing synchronization delays to swell with longer horizons. CUDA MPC observes that dependencies exist only between temporally adjacent stages and adopts local neighbor synchronization using shared atomic flags. Each block increments counters after primal updates and consensus updates, polling only the counters of neighboring blocks. This makes synchronization costs independent of the number of blocks. Convergence is mathematically guaranteed as a 1-delay bounded partially asynchronous ADMM that tolerates referencing variables from one step prior.

### V-C Memory-I/O-Aware Block Residency
Adopting FlashAttention's design philosophy, traffic to slow global memory (VRAM) is thoroughly eliminated. All optimization variables (primal, dual, and intermediate variables) reside in a fast on-chip shared memory workspace and are retained throughout the entire solve. Global memory is accessed only for initial loading at startup, writing out control inputs upon completion, and exchanging boundary variables with adjacent blocks. A resource allocation mechanism automatically determines the optimal subhorizon length $M$ and block count $B$ based on the device's shared memory and thread count limits.

captions.F2: Configuration diagram where prediction horizon $N$ is partitioned into lengths of $M$ and assigned to CUDA blocks (SMs). Fast updates occur within blocks using shared memory, while only adjacent blocks exchange boundary values and atomic sync flags via L2 cache or global memory.

sections.heading: Benchmark results: A 965x speedup and the dramatic control performance of long horizons
sections.summary: CUDA MPC achieved up to a 965x speedup over PyTorch implementations using the same ADMM scheme, slashing VRAM communication by orders of magnitude. In nonlinear benchmarks, it solved long-horizon swarm control problems in real time without collisions, where acados and CasADi either failed to compute or broke down.
sections.details:
Evaluations were conducted on a machine with an Intel Core i7-12700H and an NVIDIA RTX 3060 Laptop GPU (6 GB VRAM).

### VI-A Comparison with Tensor-Framework Implementations
To evaluate the GPU-native implementation, CUDA MPC was compared against PyTorch and Julia implementations of $\pi$MPC (which use the same parallel ADMM splitting) on an AFTI-16 aircraft model. CUDA MPC achieved speedups of 136x at horizon $N=5$, 768x at $N=1000$, and peaked at 965x at $N=50$.
The reason is clear: at $N=1000$, PyTorch triggered 172,456 internal kernel launches, whereas CUDA MPC required just 1. Furthermore, VRAM traffic was drastically reduced from 17.42 GB to 31.2 MB, and the average time per iteration dropped significantly from 0.86 ms to 0.0060 ms.

### VI-B Scalability and Closed-Loop Performance Across Nonlinear Benchmarks
Performance was evaluated across six nonlinear benchmarks: Inverted Pendulum, Cart-Pole, Car Parking with obstacle avoidance, Truck-Trailer backing, Quadrotor-Pole, and Centralized Swarm with 10 agents.

- **Solve Time Scaling**: While CPU methods like acados perform well at short horizons, their solve times explode as $N$ increases. CUDA MPC scales very mildly with horizon length. For instance, in Car Parking ($N=100$), acados takes 165.71 ms, whereas CUDA MPC finishes in just 5.75 ms (about 29x faster).
- **The True Value of Long Horizons in Closed-Loop Control**: In low-dimensional problems with sparse constraints, second-order CPU solvers excel in local convergence and show comparable or better tracking even with short horizons. However, the picture changes completely when state dimensions are high and constraints are dense. In Car Parking, CUDA MPC solved a horizon looking roughly 100 seconds ahead within a 0.1-second sampling interval, parking while directly avoiding obstacles without needing a global path from Hybrid A*.
- **Decisive Difference in 10-Agent Swarm Control**: In a scenario where 10 drones form a formation while avoiding mutual collisions ($N=100$, 100 ms period), acados (HPIPM) failed to find a feasible solution even after 3524.72 ms. CasADi (Ipopt) returned feasible solutions but took an average of 4451.42 ms (~4.5 s), making it unusable for real-time control. The GPU-based Primal-Dual iLQR was fast at 26.37 ms, but deadlocked due to collision avoidance penalties. CUDA MPC was the only solver that achieved real-time execution within the sampling interval (averaging 28.22 ms) while maintaining collision-free coordinated flight.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook
sections.summary: CUDA MPC broke through the computational barrier for long-horizon real-time MPC through co-design of algorithms and GPU hardware. Future work points to deployment and validation on real embedded GPU boards.
sections.details:
This work established "CUDA MPC," a GPU-native MPC solver co-designing parallel-in-horizon ADMM with CUDA memory and execution models. By fusing the entire iteration loop into a single kernel and utilizing on-chip shared memory, it dramatically reduced kernel launch overhead and global memory traffic, enabling real-time solves of nonlinear, densely constrained robotics problems at horizons 1 to 2 orders of magnitude longer than conventional solvers.

This demonstrates the potential to directly handle complex collision avoidance and multi-agent coordination within a single long-horizon MPC, replacing traditional hierarchical pipelines of planners and short-horizon MPCs. Future work includes implementing the solver on embedded GPUs (such as Jetson) with tighter power and memory constraints, followed by closed-loop validation on physical robotic hardware in real-world environments.

takeaways: The key to accelerating iterative optimization on GPUs lies not just in parallel computing power, but in kernel fusion and variable residency in shared memory (minimizing memory I/O)

In time-parallel optimization, replacing grid-wide synchronization barriers with lightweight atomic-flag local synchronization between adjacent blocks significantly improves scalability with respect to horizon length

While CPU second-order methods (like SQP) remain strong for simple control problems, GPU-accelerated long-horizon real-time optimization delivers breakthroughs in high-dimensional, densely constrained non-convex problems (such as swarm control and obstacle avoidance)
limitations: If the state/input dimension per stage (working set size) is too large, it exceeds the on-chip shared memory limit (S_max), preventing block residency
To allocate maximum shared memory, active blocks per SM are restricted to 1, accepting a trade-off that results in lower GPU occupancy
All experiments were conducted on a desktop-class laptop GPU (RTX 3060 Laptop); validation on low-power embedded GPUs (e.g., Jetson) onboard actual robots remains future work
